fig1_metrics_and_ceilings.svg: Three ways to score the same pair of reservoirs, kept on separate axes because their ranges have nothing in common. A power cycle is graded by $\eta=W/Q_{in}$, capped by the Carnot value (carnot_efficiency) with everything above it forbidden — efficiency_is_possible enforces the line. Run the cycle backwards and the figure of merit becomes a coefficient of performance, which is NOT capped by 1 and diverges as the two reservoirs approach each other: at $T_H=310$ K the ideal heat pump delivers 31 units of heat per unit of work. $\gamma=\beta+1$ always, because the heat pump also gets to keep the work.
fig2_isentropic_component_grading.svg: Why component losses compound in a cycle. The isentropic efficiency multiplies a turbine's output (isentropic_turbine_efficiency, turbine_work_actual) but DIVIDES into a compressor's input (isentropic_compressor_efficiency, compressor_work_actual), so the two curves bend in opposite directions away from the ideal. At $\eta=0.8$ the turbine returns 80% of its ideal work while the compressor demands 125% of its ideal input. Since the net work of a gas-turbine cycle is the difference of two large numbers, both errors eat the same margin — the back work ratio problem that Topic 9 returns to.
